transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

On your Bosch SMS25AW00G, error code E:09 specifically indicates a failure in the flow-through heating element or its circuit. This is the part responsible for heating the water during the wash and the final rinse. Regarding cost: this is not usually an extremely expensive fix because there is no gas or sealed refrigerant system involved. However, on many modern Bosch dishwashers like yours, the heater is integrated into the circulation pump assembly (the flow-through heater) rather than being a separate simple element at the bottom of the tub. This means if the heater part has failed, you typically check the entire pump/heater unit. The part itself is moderately priced, but it requires some dismantling to access. If the issue turns out to be just a wiring fault or a sensor, it would be cheaper. Before we look at parts, I need to confirm the nature of the "stone cold" symptom to rule out other possibilities. Is the entire wash water and the dishes genuinely cold to the touch when you open the door at the end of the cycle? (If they were hot but just wet, that would be a drying issue, not a heating fault.)
Yes, genuinely cold. The water and the dishes are both cold, and it's the same on the hot programme as on eco. It's been like this the last three runs.

Thank you for confirming that. Since the dishes are genuinely cold on both hot and eco programmes, and you have error code E:09, this points to a failure in the heating circuit itself. On your Bosch SMS25AW00G, there is no separate exposed heating element at the bottom of the tub. Instead, the dishwasher uses a 'flow-through' heater built directly into the circulation pump assembly (the motor that sprays the water). The E:09 code specifically indicates that this flow-through heater or its circuit has failed. The most likely cause is that the flow-through heating element inside the pump assembly has burned out. Less commonly, it could be a faulty temperature sensor giving a false reading, or a wiring issue (often in the door loom) preventing power from reaching the heater. To narrow this down safely, we need to check if the heater itself is electrically intact. Please ensure the dishwasher is switched off and unplugged (or isolated at the fuse box). You will need to access the circulation pump assembly, which typically involves removing the lower spray arm and possibly the filter housing to see the heater terminals. Once accessible, use a multimeter on the resistance setting to check across the two metal pins of the heating element. Please tell me the resistance reading you get (or if it shows 'OL' / infinity). This will tell us definitively whether the heater is broken.
I've got a multimeter so I can give that a go, but I'm not hugely confident with appliance wiring. Is it safe to do if it's unplugged and the panel is off? I'll report back the reading.

Yes, it is perfectly safe to do that as long as the appliance is completely isolated from mains power (unplugged or switched off at the fuse) and you only touch the electrical terminals of the component itself. Please go ahead with the resistance check across the heater pins and let me know what reading you get.
Okay, I've done it. The multimeter shows open circuit across the heater terminals on the pump. Does that mean the heater's dead, and is it worth fixing on a 9 year old machine?

Yes, an open circuit reading on the heater terminals suggests that the heating element inside the circulation pump assembly has failed. It is electrically dead and will not heat the water. Regarding whether it is worth fixing: for a 9-year-old Bosch dishwasher, checking the entire circulation pump/heater assembly is typically moderately expensive (part plus labour). If you are handy with tools and comfortable following dismantling instructions, doing it yourself saves significant cost. However, if you would prefer not to undertake that level of repair, given the age of the machine, it may be more practical to consider replacement. To proceed with a DIY fix, you will need to source the correct circulation pump assembly for your model (SMS25AW00G). The process involves draining any remaining water from the tub, removing the lower spray arm and filter housing to access the pump unit, disconnecting the electrical connector and plumbing connections, and swapping in the new unit. Ensure the machine is isolated at the mains before starting.
